source: CARDI book "ដំណាំស្រូវនៅកម្ពុជា" (Rice Cultivation in Cambodia), by Men Sarom, Thuy Lina and Pheng Thimuny, published by CARDI, 2007, Chapter 5 (Genetics), by Men Sarom and Kit Khunhel, sections 5.2.3-5.2.4 (Reproduction modes and breeding/selection methods). No elibrary URL visible.
text: Background on how new rice varieties (like those already profiled elsewhere in this knowledge base) are developed by breeding programs such as CARDI's. Rice reproduces sexually via self-pollinating seed (unlike vegetatively-propagated crops such as banana, sugarcane, or ginger), which is why breeding relies on controlled crossing and multi-generation selection rather than cloning. Two main breeding approaches are described: Pure-line selection, used to develop an improved variety from within an existing/traditional variety's natural genetic variation, following roughly an 8-year timeline: Year 1, collect 200-1,000 individual panicles from the source variety; Year 2, plant each selected panicle's seed in a separate row to observe individual line performance; Years 3-4, continue selecting the best-performing lines and discard inferior ones; Years 5-7, test top candidate lines for grain quality and yield stability across locations/seasons; Year 8, release and begin seed multiplication of the selected line. Hybridization (crossing two different parent varieties, e.g. 'top cross' = (A x B) x C, or 'double cross' = (A x B) x (C x D)) is used to combine desirable traits from different parents; after the first-generation cross (F1) is uniform, the second generation (F2) segregates into diverse combinations of parental traits, and breeders then use either: (a) the Pedigree method, tracking and selecting individual plants generation by generation (F2 through roughly F8) with full lineage records kept, until a stable, uniform (homozygous) line is achieved and can be tested at multiple locations; or (b) the Bulk method, growing the F2-F6 generations together as a mixed population without individual selection (letting natural/uncontrolled selection occur), then beginning individual plant selection only once the population is mostly stabilized (uniform) around the F6 generation, which requires less labor during early generations than the pedigree method but takes longer before selection can meaningfully begin.
caveat: This is background on the CARDI variety-development process rather than a farming technique itself - included as context for how varieties already documented in this knowledge base (Riang Chey, Sen Pidao, Phka Rumdoul, IR66, etc.) were originally developed. Not intended as a do-it-yourself breeding guide for farmers.
